clinicalPearls: May be congenital, often with ipsilateral renal or mesonephric duct anomalies as in Zinner syndrome, or acquired secondary to ejaculatory duct obstruction, infection or prior surgery
Located laterally, off the midline, which distinguishes it from midline mullerian duct and prostatic utricle cysts
Frequently asymptomatic; larger cysts may cause perineal discomfort, painful ejaculation, haematospermia, dysuria, or infertility
Congenital cysts commonly present between the second and fourth decades as they gradually enlarge
Transrectal ultrasound and pelvic MRI characterise the lesion and its relationship to the ejaculatory ducts and the seminal vesicle
An association with renal agenesis should always prompt a search for the complete Zinner triad
Small asymptomatic cysts are observed, whereas symptomatic ones may be aspirated or excised
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital seminal vesicle cysts result from maldevelopment of the distal mesonephric duct with atresia or obstruction of the ejaculatory duct, causing cystic dilatation of the seminal vesicle and frequently coexisting ipsilateral renal maldevelopment. Acquired cysts arise when inflammation, previous surgery or chronic obstruction impedes seminal vesicle drainage, leading to retention of secretions and progressive cystic expansion.
additionalDifferentials: Zinner syndrome when renal agenesis is present
additionalInvestigations: Transrectal ultrasound to localise and measure the cyst
Pelvic MRI for detailed anatomy and to assess contents, which may be haemorrhagic or proteinaceous
Renal tract imaging to exclude ipsilateral renal agenesis
Semen analysis if fertility is affected
Cyst aspiration for cytology or culture where infection or diagnostic uncertainty exists
Cross-sectional imaging to exclude a solid or neoplastic component
redFlags: Features suggesting infection, abscess or malignancy within or adjacent to the cyst
An associated renal anomaly with a compromised solitary kidney
Rapid growth or solid components on imaging
Refractory pain, infertility or recurrent haematospermia
reference.prognosis: Generally benign with an excellent outlook; asymptomatic cysts tend to remain stable, and symptomatic lesions usually resolve after aspiration or excision, although recurrence can follow simple aspiration.
pitfalls: Failing to look for associated renal agenesis and the full Zinner triad
Misclassifying a lateral cyst as a midline mullerian or utricle cyst
Attributing haematospermia solely to the cyst without excluding other causes
Choosing simple aspiration where recurrence is likely and excision would be more definitive
